Yes — a bounded sequence can have an uncountable number of subsequential limits.

**Construction.** Let $(q_n)_{n \geq 1}$ be an enumeration of $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$. This is a bounded sequence since every term lies in $[0,1]$.

**Claim.** The set of subsequential limits of $(q_n)$ is exactly $[0,1]$, which is uncountable.

*Every point of $[0,1]$ is a subsequential limit.* Fix any $x \in [0,1]$. Since $\mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ is dense in $[0,1]$, for each $k \geq 1$ there exists a rational $r_k \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ with $|r_k - x| < 1/k$. Each $r_k$ appears somewhere in the enumeration $(q_n)$, say $r_k = q_{n_k}$. Choosing the $n_k$ strictly increasing (which is always possible since each rational value occurs at a definite index and we can pick successive occurrences with larger indices), $(q_{n_k})$ is a subsequence of $(q_n)$ converging to $x$. Hence $x$ is a subsequential limit.

*No point outside $[0,1]$ is a subsequential limit.* Every term of $(q_n)$ lies in the closed set $[0,1]$, so any convergent subsequence has its limit in $[0,1]$.

Therefore the set of subsequential limits equals $[0,1]$, which is uncountable. ∎

**Remark.** This is consistent with the general fact that the set of subsequential limits of any sequence in a compact metric space is a nonempty closed subset of that space; closed subsets of $[0,1]$ may well be uncountable (e.g., $[0,1]$ itself, the Cantor set), so boundedness imposes no countability restriction on the set of limit points.

### PROOF COMPLETE

The problem: Can a bounded sequence have an uncountable number of subsequential limits? Justify.

Let me think. A bounded sequence in ℝ has its set of subsequential limits as a closed subset of the closure of the sequence's range. Actually, the set of subsequential limits of any sequence in a compact metric space is nonempty and closed.

A bounded sequence in ℝ: its range is bounded, so contained in some compact interval [a,b]. The set of subsequential limits is a closed subset of [a,b]. But closed subsets of ℝ can be uncountable (e.g., the Cantor set, or [0,1] itself).

So the question is whether we can construct a bounded sequence whose set of subsequential limits is uncountable.

Yes! Enumerate a dense subset of [0,1]. For instance, enumerate the rationals in [0,1] as a sequence. Then every real number in [0,1] is a subsequential limit (since rationals are dense, every real is a limit of rationals, and we can pick a subsequence converging to it). So the set of subsequential limits is all of [0,1], which is uncountable.

So the answer is YES.

Let me write a clean proof.

Proof: Yes, a bounded sequence can have an uncountable number of subsequential limits.

Construction: Let (q_n) be an enumeration of the rationals in [0,1]. This is a bounded sequence (all terms in [0,1]). For any real number x ∈ [0,1], since ℚ ∩ [0,1] is dense in [0,1], there exists a sequence of rationals in [0,1] converging to x. Each such rational appears in the enumeration (q_n), so we can select a subsequence converging to x. Hence every x ∈ [0,1] is a subsequential limit. Since [0,1] is uncountable, the set of subsequential limits is uncountable.

Conversely, one might note the set of subsequential limits is always closed, but that's not needed for the answer—the question just asks whether it's possible.

Actually let me also note: the set of subsequential limits is exactly [0,1] here. Any subsequential limit must lie in [0,1] since all terms are in [0,1] and [0,1] is closed. And we showed every point of [0,1] is achieved. So the set equals [0,1].

This is a complete justification.
